article.title: “Disaster Waiting to Happen”: Iowa Declares Emergency as U.S. Army Detonates 5 Tons of Lead Azide
article.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report . I’m Amy Goodman. Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds has declared a disaster emergency in three counties as the U.S. Army prepares to detonate nearly five tons of highly unstable lead-based explosives at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa today. The detonation will cause a massive blast that could send toxic lead dust spewing across communities, farmland, and potentially into the Mississippi River. The detonation is scheduled for 9 a.m. Central Time. Officials have recommended residents of Middletown, where the plant is located, and anyone within a five-mile cone southwest of the plant to evacuate, while people living up to 20 miles away have been told to stay indoors with their windows closed. Men are being told to — in this farmland area, to bring their cows inside. A number of farmers have said that’s impossible. Jeremy Atwater, a resident of Augusta, Iowa, told a reporter he plans to go west to escape the toxic plume. JEREMY ATWATER : But now the winds are changing directions, and it’s going to blow directly south through our town, so I guess we’re going to head west instead. REPORTER : And what’s out west? Is it hotels? Or is it just — JEREMY ATWATER : Anything but the bomb. … My primary concern is a lot. I mean, nobody really knows. There’s never been a documented explosion like this, as far as I could find any doing my due diligence digging in the interweb. But it’s just going to be a big problem. It’s going to be a lot of lead poisoning going on. AMY GOODMAN : The Army published an updated map estimating the lead plume could spread all the way to northern Missouri, more than 100 miles from ground zero. There’s no safe level of lead exposure. Lead is a neurotoxin that can cause permanent cognitive and behavioral harm and is particularly dangerous to children and pregnant women. The Army says the explosives, stored for decades in 68 drums at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, have deteriorated to the point that they could spontaneously explode. This is acting Army Secretary Adam Telle speaking at a press conference in Iowa Tuesday. ARMY SECRETARY ADAM TELLE : There is consensus across the experts across the country that a controlled, mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is far preferable to uncontrolled, spontaneous detonation of that substance. AMY GOODMAN : On Saturday, The New York Times published an investigation revealing the Army had initially pursued another, cleaner option, a chemical process designed to neutralize the explosives without a blast. In March, the Army awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based company that uses a sulfur-based solution to break down explosives and immobilize toxic chemicals. Two months later, the Army canceled the contract and chose detonation instead. Well, for more, we go to Lexington Park, Maryland, where we’re joined by Pat Elder, the founder of the group Military Poisons. He just wrote a piece headlined “The Pentagon’s Toxic Shortcut in Iowa Is a Warning to the World.” Pat Elder, welcome back to Democracy Now! Iowans are panicked. PAT ELDER : Thank you. AMY GOODMAN : They say they have gotten very little notice about what’s about to take place. If there are hills, they’re saying people are heading to the hills. But what do they do with their cows, those who are farmers? If you could start off by saying why you see this as a warning to the world? And how on Earth did this surprise this whole community, where the governor now has declared a disaster emergency in three counties? PAT ELDER : Well, thank you for having me, Amy. I appreciate it. We have to go back to the words of Thomas Jefferson, who wrote in the Declaration of Independence that we must be warned of usurpations by the federal government that will strip the liberties of individual states. And so, that’s what we see today. The Army has decided to act as it wishes, and it is going against the recommendations of its own experts and experts with the EPA and experts with the Applied Physics Lab, Johns Hopkins here in Maryland. There is no reason for this to be done, and it is a disaster waiting to happen. And I feel sorry for the poor folks in Iowa, as I do for people around the world who suffer these same sorts of fates, because the United States Army does what it wants and has acted in a Neanderthal fashion with its detonation and supposed disposal of hazardous materials. AMY GOODMAN : Let’s talk about the effects — PAT ELDER : I think it’s — AMY GOODMAN : — of lead, Pat Elder. If you can talk about the health concerns for lead exposure, especially for children and fetuses? The New York Times says lead is a neurotoxin, and there are no safe levels for exposure. Can you take it from there? PAT ELDER : Well, I can, Amy. Thank you so much. We know, all the way from our experiences with leaded gas and lead paint, and the fiasco in Flint, Michigan — we have the clinical data — we understand that lead is a killer. It is a killer in the embryo. It is a killer for young children. And it is a killer for all of us. But the Army would pretend that this is not the case, because — well, because it’s very fond of lead in ammunition. And so, we look around the country, and we see where the Army has been absolutely irresponsible in the way that it handles lead. We look at Fort Ord in California, for instance, and entire sand dunes are loaded with lead, and campers are allowed to traipse. They built an entire campus at the University of California, Monterey Bay, over top of old Army buildings with lead pipes. The poor kids are drinking lead. The Army is irresponsible when it comes to lead all around the world. It has buried it, and it has — supposed to be following a process, that it does not follow, to safely dispose of lead. AMY GOODMAN : So, let’s — PAT ELDER : And I want to add, too — AMY GOODMAN : Go ahead. PAT ELDER : Yeah, thanks. Just, you know, we’re not just dealing with lead here. We’re dealing with lead azide. And the best way to put this into focus is that lead azide is the explosive that detonates a bomb. So, if we have a 2,000-pound bomb that is falling on Gaza, lead azide the size of a small pea is detonated, which then sends a tremendous blast into the bomb itself. So, it is the explosive agent. And this is the material the Army is getting ready to detonate. And so, we’re not just talking about lead itself. We’re also talking about contaminations like hydrogen cyanide and hydrazoic acid. These are deadly. They deprive the brain of oxygen. And this is what is getting unleashed on the people of Iowa. AMY GOODMAN : I want to ask you about that New York Times exposé on Saturday that may have surprised many, as so much of this has just crept up on them, the people of the community. It’s not as if this is a story that broke into the whole, you know, country. But they’ve been dealing with it for a while. Many residents did not know until the last few days what was about to happen. But The New York Times published an investigation revealing the Army had initially pursued another, cleaner option: a chemical process designed to neutralize the explosives without a blast. In March, the Army awarded this contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based company that uses a sulfur-based solution to break down explosives and immobilize toxic chemicals. Two months later, the Army canceled the contract and chose detonation instead. Pat Elder, explain. PAT ELDER : Well, we have to go back to March of 2025 to fully understand what has transpired. The Army itself, along with experts from the EPA and experts with the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Lab here in Maryland, sat down, and they all voted that it would be too dangerous to detonate these materials, and that the way to do it is to saturate the exterior of these barrels, and the interior of these barrels once they are opened, with a chemical compound that is made of sulfur in water. And so, we spray that over the barrels. And when the Army says, “Well, this is too dangerous,” MuniRem, the company behind this process, has said that it would use robots, as it has in decontaminating other Army ammunition sites. So, the entire process and the entire culmination in the Army deciding suddenly that they would go ahead and detonate this material is lunacy. And the idea that way back in August of 2025, we — the Army knew that there was a problem, and MuniRem knew there was a problem, and Johns Hopkins knew, and the EPA knew. The last people to find out are the people of Iowa and the people that live in the immediate area. They didn’t find out until last week. And that’s how the Army operates. AMY GOODMAN : Pat Elder, I want to thank you for being with us, founder of the group Military Poisons. We’ll link to your piece , “The Pentagon’s Toxic Shortcut in Iowa Is a Warning to the World.” Coming up, Egyptian writer Abdelrahman ElGendy. He just won the National Book Award for Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming , but he wasn’t at the award ceremony. The U.S. denied ElGendy a visa. While he was a political prisoner in Egypt, starting when he was 17 years old, he published his writings in the Egyptian independent paper Mada Masr . Right now we are awaiting a court’s decision, an appeal of the government’s just closing down Mada Masr . We’ll go to Cairo, as well. Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : “Massive Will” by Emel Mathlouthi, performing in our Democracy Now! studio. To see all the performances and interviews in our Democracy Now! studios of musicians and artists, go to democracynow.org .
